description: I am a 2nd-year Space and Satellite Technology student at USTH. I am competing solo to challenge myself in Orbital Mechanics and Mission Design. My project focuses on solving the soft-landing simulation problem for the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge, with the goal of developing an orbital simulation algorithm packaged into an interactive Web App.
summary: We built a decision-support tool for choosing a lunar south pole landing site among four candidates (Site01, Site04, Site07, Site11). Using NASA LOLA DEM and slope rasters at 5 m per pixel, we scored the terrain of each region of interest (ROI): slope statistics and flat-area share. We then used SPICE ephemerides (DE440s) to compute, hour by hour for one year from 1 Dec 2026, when the Sun and Earth are above both the horizon and the local DEM terrain horizon. From these we derived continuous windows when an ROI is both sunlit and in line of sight to Earth, and ranked the sites with a weighted score (terrain, sunlight, Earth visibility, longest window). Site07 ranks first, with a median slope of 1.6° and a longest window of 301 hours. Site11 is nearly tied. An interactive 3D model shows the Sun, Earth and Moon at true scale, site terrain with shadows, and a year-long time slider. It helps mission planners compare sites transparently.
details:
What it does

Our tool helps mission planners choose a lunar south pole landing site among four candidates (Site01, Site04, Site07, Site11). It works in four steps:

  1. Terrain analysis. We score each region of interest (ROI) on slope statistics (median, 90th and 95th percentile, share of area under 5° and 10°) and area.
  2. Sun and Earth visibility. For every hour of one year (from 1 Dec 2026, UTC), we compute the elevation of the Sun and Earth for an observer 2 m above the ROI. A body counts as visible only if it is above 0° and above the local terrain horizon, which we ray-cast from the DEM (360 azimuths, out to 8 km).
  3. Favourable windows. We find continuous periods of 24 hours or more when the Sun and Earth are both visible, which matters for power and communication.
  4. Ranking. A weighted score combines terrain (30%), sunlight (25%), both visible (25%) and longest window (20%). We tested three weight sets for stability.

Results

Site07 (Peak Near Shackleton) ranks first: median slope 1.58°, 99.2% of its ROI under 5°, both Sun and Earth visible 26.5% of the year, longest window 301 hours. Site11 is nearly tied, and their order changes with the weights. Site01 and Site04 rank third and fourth under all three weight sets.

Benefits and impact

The tool makes site comparison transparent and repeatable. Anyone can see why a site ranks where it does, and can change the weights or add sites. It supports early mission planning, where sunlight and Earth line-of-sight windows drive power, thermal and communication design.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA LOLA DEM and slope rasters (5 m per pixel), ROI shapefiles, SPICE kernels (DE440s ephemeris, lunar frame kernels).
  • Python in Google Colab: rasterio, geopandas, pyproj, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, spiceypy.
  • Web: an interactive 3D page in HTML/JavaScript with Three.js and SVG charts.

Creativity

  • The visibility check combines SPICE geometry with the real DEM horizon, not just the geometric elevation.
  • The 3D model shows the Sun, Earth and Moon at true scale on their real orbits, and you can zoom from the Moon’s surface out to the whole system. The Moon’s orientation is fitted to the SPICE directions.
  • For each site, the model shows real terrain with shadows computed from the DEM at the selected time, plus a year-long time slider linked to charts, a monthly heatmap and the ranking table.

Limitations we considered

Results are preliminary and not cross-checked against an independent source. Terrain shadowing uses only a 16 × 16 km DEM around each site, so results are slightly optimistic. The ranking weights were chosen by our team. The Site04 ROI is only about 0.26 ha, the smallest of the four. The Moon, Earth and Sun surface textures in the 3D view are procedural illustrations, not imagery.
